title: Teachers Willie Foster and Philip Boyto, and a day job
summary: Willie Foster taught him banjo, then Philip Boyto after Foster left, while he worked for United Fruit; he describes developing a style like Earl Hines.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: So you brought us up to date on that now, all through your life. Who, who was your teacher? Willie Foster, he was there, right at 510 Coen Street. He was my first teacher.
He was playing on, uh, on, uh, for Stratford, on that boat out there, you know, in the river Presidents. And what instrument did he teach you?

He taught me banjo. He taught me banjo, he taught Kimball's banjo, he taught Sales's banjo. But I was the last one that he taught. How old were you then? Well that's where I got the figure out. And Philip Boito, you know, got the music still down there. I took, when Willie Foster went back to St. Louis, he played up there. Well, we still worked for St. Louis, you know, the Boots used to leave town and go up there. Well, I got another teacher, he was at GC Coins, he was on Cronley Street then. Philip Boito, he used to teach me. I had my lunch hour. Well, I was working, I started working for the United Fruit Company, 321 Cent, Charles Street, on delivering money from that office to the Winner Central Bank. I used to work on the money bank, you know. You see, and we used to go to Celeste Street, walk and pick up the money. They had five boats at that time, the Ellis, the Cortego, Alvangaris, and the Copper name, you know, the boats where we used to go there and pick up the money, automobiles and bring back then. I was relieved the elevator guy. Well, I got a job running on a boat, going to Camden, Arkansas. Well, I just gave up that job. And I started playing with it. All full time.
What did Willie Foster teach you? How did he teach you the language?

He taught me the rhythms of it there, from the bottom of it. He taught me melody and chords, and I developed a style of my own, similar to Earl Hines. Well, like Earl Hines played piano. I adopted it like that. I got the idea, well I didn't get all of it, but I got a lot of him, but more of me. More of Al, you know what I mean? Well, he got the idea, he stole from Louis Armstrong, that's what Louis Hines did. So, I got the idea from him, of course I played a chord instrument just like he did. And then, as the years went on, I swung the guitar. Well, I happened to be in the Groomwolf, and one day, Rippin' with Santo, the drum lift, and Mr. Alec Hillsbury, coming there with this man to donate all this money. What's his name?
